newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - Japan's communists on the rise.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Japan's communists on the rise.

text.p: What's in a name?
Riding high after huge gains in Tokyo elections this month, Japan's Communist Party (JCP) thinks names mean a lot.

So the party does not plan to change its name, despite the image it conjures up of an outdated ideology. It believes that political parties in Japan that have changed their name in recent years are now paying the price.

JCP Central Committee chairman Tetsuzo Fuwa told Reuters in an interview that election results for the Tokyo Municipal Assembly, in which the party doubled its share to 26 seats, showed the communists were now the only real opposition to the ruling Liberal Democrat Party (LDP).
"In terms of political strength, we have entered into an era where we can fight elections facing off against the LDP itself," Fuwa said.
He said the dismal failure of the New Frontier Party, which won no seats, and the Social Democrats, whose 29-seat share shrank to just one, reflected public distrust and political infighting.
"It was self destruction. People don't trust the Social Democrats because they went to bed with the LDP... And faction fighting within the New Frontier Party meant they got wiped out," he said.
"The parties who haven't changed their name and their policies -- the LDP and the Communists -- are the only ones who are doing well."
COMMUNIST BOOM IS NO SURPRISE
Political analyst Minoru Morita said the communist boom is no surprise.

"The results of the Tokyo elections were as expected. At both the national and local levels, the other parties' policies have become so much the same that only the communists are left in opposition," he said.
"The JCP is the only political party capable of marshalling -- and monopolising -- the votes of the one in three people who are against the government."

The communists' campaign against an increase in the sales tax, unpopular changes to the national health and pension systems, and billion-yen payouts to salvage busted companies all contributed to a JCP boom, Morita added.
Following a doubling of its seats in national lower house elections last year, the communists hope for another big win in next year's upper house elections.

A major factor in the JCP's popularity is its squeaky-clean image in a land where corruption in politics and big business has pushed public patience beyond the breaking point, said Keio University political science professor Taizo Yakushiji.
"The absence of corruption in the JCP is a big plus. The public has lost confidence in the Liberal Democrats and the other parties because of corruption scandals," he said.
But Yakushiji said the JCP's honeymoon with public opinion -- due, he says, to the absence of a coherent opposition and voter anger against the ruling LDP -- will not last.

"Once the other opposition parties come through this transition phase the JCP won't do so well. And right now a lot of people support the communists because they're angry with the government, but they'll go back later," he said.

The number of floating voters, disillusioned with the previous mainstream political parties, is steadily rising and will be the key to the JCP's performance in next year's general elections, JCP leader Fuwa said.
DEBATE ABOUT CHANGE OF NAME
"The non-affiliated people are those who have until now supported conservative parties but who find themselves saying, 'It can't go on'," he said.
"The change is like a snowball -- the more people look at what's around them, the greater the numbers of non-affiliated voters will grow. The Communist Party will combine with these people."

However, Morita said one major obstacle to the communists taking power, or at least a sizeable chunk of power in one of the world's richest capitalist nations, was its name and its association with discredited East European communist parties.
"People still feel this kind of allergy to the word," Morita said.
However, Fuwa said the party's name will not change to pander to voters, and there are signs that voters are becoming used to it.

"We want people to see that we feel responsible for our past and present actions and what we will do in the future. As people are realising that, the number of people insisting we don't change the name is increasing."
